These guys whoop it up, playing Baseball and horseshoes at the 'Lithuanian Country Club'. No women around what soever! They look to be having a grand time, in their rayon slacks... The cameraman looks to have a little fun too, claudestinely taping the men as they enter and exit the latrine! Oh BOYS! The film 'ends' but just keeps on going! Soon we're headed down to 'South Park' to have ourselves a time, we witness a baseball game, more horseshoes, and lots of men…

The Great War was over, we'd made the world safe for democracy, this was the heartland of America: Allegheny County, Illinois, to be exact, and it was time for all the supervisors of the steelmill to have an early summer picnic. The "Lithuanian Country Club" was chosen-- basically a verdant eden with a shack plopped into the middle of it, looking like a set from THE TEXAS CHAINSAW MASSACRE. One by one, these codgers show up for this picnic, stogies in teeth, fedoras on head, and belts cinched above the navel. Apparently there were no female "supervisors" at this gig, because it's an all-stag…

Oh my god. Too think I've seen it all on this site, I then have the pleasure of seeing 'The Chicken Of Tomorrow'. Trust me, this film will take you off your feed for a week. Narrated by Lowell Thomas. It starts out by him intoning "Did you know that poultry is the nation's third largest crop" in such a way that it's hard to figure out whether he's very bored or very excited. And THEN, the fun starts as we see chickens, dead and spread eagled on the production line in the hundreds. The whole film is about the farmer's never ending quest to find a better chicken, and we see a contest to see who…

Lowell Thomas has a building named after him at a college in my hometown (Marist College- Poughkeepsie, NY). I don't think that narrating crap like this helped him earn that! This film has relatively high camp value however, and the 'Chicken of Tomorrow Queen' is a highlight from this film that I particularly enjoy...

Vomit of tomorrow night. This film does everything possible to make chicken appear completely unappetizing. Bleccch. Unfortunately, it's also really slow going. And the terrible script is an insult to Lowell Thomas' talents (and it sounds like he knows it). Worth watching for the "ugh" factor, but prepare for some long, boring stretches...

the_ape: Dr. Bernard Adrian is a kindly scientist who seeks to cure a young woman's polio. He needs human spinal fluid to complete the formula for his experimental serum. Meanwhile, a vicious circus ape has broken out of its cage, and is terrorizing the townspeople. Can there be a connection?

rv: Jump to the scene where Karloff demonstrates his theories to a suspicious investigator by showing him two guinea pigs that he sets on the table. Keep your eye on the one on the right! All in all, this is a good little picture, with Karloff in typically fine form as the well-meaning, sympathetic scientist driven to dark deeds by circumstances and coincidences beyond his control.

The guinea pig scene was... beyond words. Familiar plot: misunderstood scientist who becomes overly zealous in the quest to save mankind. But in spite of (or because of) his dubious methods, mankind benefits, while the only satisfaction afforded the "mad" scientist is in seeing his theory proven, albeit at a cost not all will accept as justified.

The Ape presents the standard tale of a ethically challenged physician searching for the cure to a crippling, deadly disease. His 25-year single-minded quest, exacerbated by the loss of his daughter and wife to the 'paralysis' (resembling polio, though never named), drives him to murder for the key ingredient to a cure. A killer ape, escaped from a circus, invades his home. He kills it and disguises himself as the ape, which is his eventual undoing, in order to hunt his victim. Good performances, a few laughs, the Jekyll and Hyde metaphor and an unusual ending with a questionable moral make…
Rather Sweet for a Horror Film

Boris Karloff (Dr. Bernard Adrian) plays a doctor whose desire to find a cure for a paralysis disease - resembling polio - get the best of his moral compass - particularly after seeing positive results in his attempt to cure Maris Wrixon (Frances Clifford). His descent into serial murder and success with his patient does not help him in the end. Karloff shows off his sweet temperament here to great effect. The rest of the cast are adequate. The plot is nothing great, but serviceable for a "B" movies script - it gets the job done and the cautionary tale told.
